name: BMI
description: Computes Body Mass Index as weight÷(height in metres)², dividing weight in kg by height squared. Height is entered in cm and converted internally by dividing by 100.
notes: Enter height in cm (the formula divides by 100 to get metres). BMI is a population screening tool and does not distinguish muscle from fat.

name: Max heart rate
description: Estimates the maximum heart rate in beats per minute using the common formula 220−age. It gives an age-based ceiling used to set exercise intensity zones.
notes: This is a rough population estimate that can be off by 10-20 bpm for an individual. For precise limits, an exercise stress test is needed.

name: Ideal weight (BMI 22)
description: Computes the body weight corresponding to a BMI of 22 for a given height, using 22×(height in metres)². Height in cm is converted to metres by dividing by 100.
notes: Enter height in cm. BMI 22 is a common midpoint of the healthy range; the ideal figure is a guideline, not a strict target.

name: Daily calories
description: Estimates total daily energy expenditure by multiplying basal metabolic rate (bmr) by an activity factor. The result is the calories needed to maintain weight, in kcal per day.
notes: The activity factor typically ranges from about 1.2 (sedentary) to 1.9 (very active); the default 1.5 is moderate. Requires a BMR value as input.

name: Body surface area (Mosteller)
description: Estimates total body surface area with the Mosteller formula, as the square root of height in centimeters times weight in kilograms divided by 3600. It is widely used for drug dosing and physiological normalization.
notes: Height must be in centimeters and weight in kilograms, giving area in square meters. It is an empirical estimate that does not account for body composition or shape.

name: BMR (Mifflin, female)
description: Estimates the daily basal metabolic rate for women using the Mifflin-St Jeor equation from weight, height, and age. It gives the calories the body burns at complete rest to maintain basic functions.
notes: Weight in kg, height in cm, age in years; the −161 constant is specific to females. Multiply by an activity factor to estimate total daily energy expenditure.

name: BMR (Harris-Benedict, male)
description: Estimates the daily basal metabolic rate for men using the original Harris-Benedict equation from weight, height, and age. It represents the resting energy needed to sustain vital functions.
notes: Weight in kg, height in cm, age in years. This is the classic 1919 formula, which tends to run slightly higher than the newer Mifflin-St Jeor equation.

name: BMR (Harris-Benedict, female)
description: Estimates the daily basal metabolic rate for women using the original Harris-Benedict equation from weight, height, and age. It gives the calories burned at rest to maintain basic bodily functions.
notes: Weight in kg, height in cm, age in years; the coefficients are specific to females. As the 1919 formula it typically reads a bit higher than Mifflin-St Jeor.

name: Max heart rate (Tanaka)
description: Estimates maximum heart rate from age with the Tanaka formula, 208 minus 0.7 times age. It is considered more accurate across a wide age range than the older 220-minus-age rule.
notes: Age is in years and the result is a population average in beats per minute; individual maxima can vary by roughly ±10 bpm. It is an estimate, not a substitute for a measured stress test.

name: Target heart rate (Karvonen)
description: Computes a training target heart rate by the Karvonen method, taking the heart-rate reserve (max minus resting) times the desired intensity and adding the resting rate back. It personalizes target zones using resting heart rate.
notes: Intensity is a fraction between 0 and 1 (e.g. 0.7 for 70%), not a percentage. Accuracy depends on correct maximum and resting heart rate values.

name: VO2max estimate (heart rate)
description: Estimates maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max) from the ratio of maximum to resting heart rate, scaled by 15.3. A lower resting heart rate relative to maximum indicates greater aerobic fitness.
notes: Result is in mL/kg/min and is a rough estimate; it needs accurate max and resting heart rates. Direct or field-test measurements are more reliable than this heart-rate ratio method.

name: VO2max (Cooper test)
description: Estimates maximal oxygen uptake from the distance run in 12 minutes using the Cooper test formula, (distance − 504.9)/44.73. Greater distance covered corresponds to higher aerobic capacity.
notes: Distance must be in meters run in exactly 12 minutes at maximal effort. The result in mL/kg/min is an estimate that assumes an all-out, evenly paced run.

name: Running pace
description: Computes running pace as time divided by distance, giving the minutes needed to cover each kilometer. A smaller value means a faster pace.
notes: With time in minutes and distance in kilometers, the result is minutes per kilometer. This is the inverse of speed, so lower is faster, not slower.

name: Calories burned (MET)
description: Estimates energy expended during activity as the MET value times body weight in kilograms times duration in hours. Higher-intensity activities have larger MET values and burn more calories.
notes: This form uses the approximation that 1 MET ≈ 1 kcal per kg per hour. Weight is in kg and time in hours; MET values are tabulated per activity.

name: Daily water intake
description: Estimates a daily fluid intake target as body weight in kilograms times 35, giving milliliters per day. It follows the common guideline of about 35 mL of water per kilogram of body weight.
notes: This is a general rule of thumb; actual needs vary with climate, activity, and health, and food provides some water too. Weight in kg gives the result in milliliters.

name: Ideal weight (Devine, male)
description: Estimates ideal body weight for men with the Devine formula, 50 kg plus 2.3 kg for each inch of height over 5 feet. It is used mainly for clinical drug dosing rather than as a fitness ideal.
notes: Height must be entered in inches; only inches above 60 (5 feet) add weight. It is a dosing heuristic, not a health or aesthetic target, and ignores build and body composition.

name: One-rep max (Epley)
description: Estimates the one-repetition maximum (the heaviest liftable once) using the Epley formula, weight times (1 + reps/30). It converts a submaximal set into a projected single-rep strength value.
notes: Most accurate for a moderate number of reps (roughly under 10); accuracy falls off at very high rep counts. Weight can be in any unit and the result matches that unit.

name: Calories from macronutrients
description: Computes total food energy from macronutrient grams using the Atwater factors: 4 kcal per gram of carbohydrate and protein, and 9 kcal per gram of fat. It gives the calorie content of a food or meal.
notes: Inputs are grams of each macronutrient. Alcohol (about 7 kcal/g) and fiber effects are not included in this simplified form.

name: Waist-to-height ratio
description: Computes the waist-to-height ratio by dividing waist circumference by height. It is a simple indicator of central fat distribution, with values around 0.5 or below generally considered healthier.
notes: Waist and height must be measured in the same unit so the ratio is dimensionless. It is a screening indicator, not a diagnosis, and thresholds vary by population.

name: Weight loss from calorie deficit
description: Estimates body-fat mass lost from a total calorie deficit by dividing it by 7700, the approximate calories stored in one kilogram of body fat. A larger cumulative deficit predicts more weight lost.
notes: The 7700 kcal/kg figure is an approximation, and real loss also includes water and lean tissue changes. Deficit is the cumulative total, not a daily value.

name: Steps to distance
description: Converts a step count into distance walked by multiplying steps by stride length and dividing by 1000 to give kilometers. Longer strides cover more distance per step.
notes: Stride length is in meters per step, so steps times stride gives meters, divided by 1000 for kilometers. Stride varies with height and walking speed.

name: Body Surface Area (Du Bois)
description: Estimates body surface area with the Du Bois formula from weight and height, using their fractional powers. The result in square meters is widely used for drug dosing and physiological indexing.
notes: Weight must be in kilograms and height in centimeters; the constant is calibrated to those units. It is an empirical estimate and may be less accurate at extremes of body size.

name: Body Surface Area (Haycock)
description: Estimates body surface area with the Haycock formula from weight and height raised to fixed powers. It is often preferred for children and infants and gives a result in square meters.
notes: Weight is in kilograms and height in centimeters. As an empirical regression it can differ slightly from Du Bois or Mosteller estimates for the same person.

name: Creatinine Clearance (Cockcroft-Gault, Female)
description: Estimates creatinine clearance in females by the Cockcroft-Gault equation from age, weight, and serum creatinine, including the 0.85 female correction factor. It approximates renal function for drug dosing.
notes: Weight in kilograms and serum creatinine in mg/dL; the 0.85 factor applies to females only. It estimates clearance, not measured GFR, and is unreliable at extremes of body weight or unstable creatinine.

name: Creatinine Clearance from Urine
description: Computes measured creatinine clearance from a timed urine collection, as urine creatinine times urine volume divided by serum creatinine and collection time. It is a direct measure of glomerular filtration.
notes: Urine and serum creatinine must use the same concentration unit so they cancel. Accuracy depends on a complete, accurately timed urine collection; volume and time units set the result units.

name: eGFR (MDRD, simplified)
description: Estimates the glomerular filtration rate with the simplified MDRD equation from serum creatinine and age, each raised to a negative power. The result is normalized to a body surface area of 1.73 square meters.
notes: This reduced form omits sex and race adjustment factors that the full MDRD applies; serum creatinine is in mg/dL. It is less reliable at near-normal GFR values.

name: Corrected Calcium
description: Corrects a measured serum calcium level for low albumin, adding 0.8 mg/dL for every 1 g/dL that albumin falls below 4 g/dL. It estimates the calcium level that would be seen at normal albumin.
notes: Calcium is in mg/dL and albumin in g/dL, matching the 4.0 reference and 0.8 slope. It only adjusts for albumin binding and does not replace ionized calcium measurement.

name: Anion Gap
description: Calculates the serum anion gap by subtracting the measured anions chloride and bicarbonate from sodium. It reflects unmeasured anions and helps classify metabolic acidosis.
notes: All electrolytes are in mmol/L (equivalent to mEq/L for these monovalent ions). This version excludes potassium; a low albumin lowers the apparent gap and may need correction.

name: Anion Gap (with Potassium)
description: Calculates the anion gap including potassium, subtracting chloride and bicarbonate from the sum of sodium and potassium. Adding potassium raises the gap slightly versus the sodium-only version.
notes: All values in mmol/L. Because potassium is included, the normal reference range is a few units higher than for the potassium-free anion gap.

name: Shock Index
description: Computes the shock index as heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure. Higher values indicate hemodynamic instability, with a normal range of roughly 0.5 to 0.7.
notes: Heart rate is in beats per minute and systolic pressure in mmHg; the ratio is dimensionless. It is a screening trend rather than a diagnosis and can be skewed by medications affecting heart rate.

name: IV Drip Rate
description: Determines the intravenous infusion rate in drops per minute, multiplying the fluid volume by the tubing drop factor and dividing by the infusion time. It sets how fast to run a gravity drip.
notes: Volume in mL, drop factor in drops/mL from the tubing set, and time in minutes. Using the wrong drop factor (macro vs micro drip) will give a badly incorrect rate.

name: Infusion Rate
description: Computes the continuous infusion rate in mL per hour by dividing the total fluid volume by the infusion time. It is the pump setting needed to deliver the volume over the intended period.
notes: Volume is in mL and time in hours to give mL/h directly. Ensure the time is total infusion duration, not a per-dose interval.

name: Dose by Weight
description: Calculates a total drug dose by multiplying the dose per kilogram by the patient's body weight. It is the standard weight-based dosing calculation.
notes: Dose per kg in mg/kg and weight in kg give a total in mg. Confirm whether dosing should use actual, ideal, or adjusted body weight for the specific drug.

name: Dose by Body Surface Area
description: Calculates a total drug dose by multiplying the dose per square meter by the patient's body surface area. This BSA-based approach is common in chemotherapy and pediatric dosing.
notes: Dose per m^2 in mg/m^2 and body surface area in m^2 give a total in mg. The BSA itself must be computed separately by a formula such as Du Bois or Mosteller.

name: Pediatric Dose (Clark's Rule)
description: Estimates a pediatric drug dose by Clark's rule, scaling the adult dose by the child's weight divided by 70 kg. It approximates a child dose from an adult reference by body weight.
notes: Child weight in kg and the 70 kg standard adult weight; adult dose sets the output unit. It is a rough historical estimate and modern weight-based mg/kg dosing is generally preferred.

name: Pediatric Dose (Young's Rule)
description: Estimates a pediatric drug dose by Young's rule, scaling the adult dose by age divided by age plus 12. It approximates a child dose from an adult reference using age.
notes: Child age in years; the adult dose sets the output unit. It is an age-based approximation intended for children and is not recommended for infants or over age 12.

name: Ideal Body Weight (Devine, Male)
description: Estimates ideal body weight for males by the Devine formula, starting at 50 kg and adding 2.3 kg for each inch of height above 60 inches. It is used mainly for medication dosing.
notes: Height must be in inches; the result is in kilograms. The formula is undefined in a meaningful sense below 60 inches, where it would return values at or below the 50 kg base.

name: Ideal Body Weight (Devine, Female)
description: Estimates ideal body weight for females by the Devine formula, starting at 45.5 kg and adding 2.3 kg for each inch of height above 60 inches. It is commonly used for drug dose calculations.
notes: Height is in inches and the result in kilograms; the base weight is lower than the male version. Below 60 inches it returns values at or under the 45.5 kg base and has limited validity.

name: Lean Body Mass (Boer, Female)
description: Estimates lean body mass in females by the Boer formula from weight and height, using fixed coefficients and a constant offset. It approximates the non-fat mass of the body in kilograms.
notes: Weight in kg and height in cm, matching the calibrated coefficients. It is a population regression and may be inaccurate at obesity extremes or in athletes.

name: Blood Alcohol Concentration (Widmark)
description: Estimates blood alcohol concentration by the Widmark equation from grams of alcohol consumed, body weight, and the distribution factor, then subtracts 0.015% per hour of metabolism. The result is a percentage.
notes: Alcohol in grams, weight in kg, and the Widmark factor is roughly 0.68 for men and 0.55 for women. It is an approximation that ignores absorption phase and individual metabolic variation.

name: QTc (Bazett)
description: Corrects the QT interval for heart rate using Bazett's formula, dividing the QT interval by the square root of the RR interval. It normalizes QT to a heart rate of 60 beats per minute.
notes: QT and RR are both in seconds, so QTc is also in seconds. Bazett over-corrects at fast heart rates and under-corrects at slow rates compared with other formulas.

name: QTc (Fridericia)
description: Corrects the QT interval for heart rate using Fridericia's formula, dividing the QT interval by the cube root of the RR interval. It normalizes QT and is more accurate than Bazett at extreme heart rates.
notes: QT and RR are in seconds, giving QTc in seconds. The cube-root correction reduces the rate dependence errors seen with Bazett at very fast or slow rates.

name: Parkland Formula (Burn Fluid)
description: Estimates the total crystalloid fluid needed in the first 24 hours after a burn by the Parkland formula, as 4 mL times body weight times the percent of body surface burned. It guides burn resuscitation.
notes: Weight in kg and burned area as a percent of total body surface area. Half the total is given over the first 8 hours from the time of injury and the rest over the next 16 hours.

name: Sodium Deficit
description: Estimates the amount of sodium needed to raise serum sodium to a target, as the sodium gap times total body water (0.6 times weight). It guides correction of hyponatremia.
notes: Sodium values in mmol/L and weight in kg; the 0.6 factor is total body water fraction and is lower in women and the elderly. Correct sodium slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination.

name: Free Water Deficit
description: Estimates the free water deficit in hypernatremia, as total body water (0.6 times weight) times the fractional excess of serum sodium above the normal 140. The result is the water volume needed to normalize sodium.
notes: Weight in kg and sodium in mmol/L; the result is in liters. The 0.6 body water fraction should be reduced for women and the elderly, and sodium should be lowered gradually.

name: Serum Osmolality
description: Calculates estimated serum osmolality from sodium, glucose, and BUN, doubling sodium and adding glucose over 18 and BUN over 2.8. It approximates the osmotic concentration of blood.
notes: Sodium in mmol/L, glucose and BUN in mg/dL; the divisors convert those to mmol/L contributions. Comparing this to measured osmolality gives the osmolal gap.

name: Effective Serum Osmolality
description: Calculates effective serum osmolality (tonicity) from sodium and glucose, doubling sodium and adding glucose over 18, omitting urea. It reflects the osmoles that actually drive water shifts across cell membranes.
notes: Sodium in mmol/L and glucose in mg/dL. Urea is excluded because it crosses membranes freely and does not contribute to effective osmotic force.

name: Corrected Sodium for Hyperglycemia
description: Corrects measured sodium for hyperglycemia, adding 1.6 mmol/L for each 100 mg/dL that glucose exceeds 100. It estimates the true sodium once the osmotic dilution from high glucose is accounted for.
notes: Sodium in mmol/L and glucose in mg/dL. The 1.6 factor is a common convention; some use 2.4, which yields a higher corrected value at very high glucose.

name: Maintenance Fluids (Holliday-Segar, >20kg)
description: Computes daily maintenance fluid requirement for patients over 20 kg by the Holliday-Segar method, as 1500 mL plus 20 mL for each kilogram above 20. The result is the 24-hour fluid volume.
notes: Weight in kg and this branch applies only above 20 kg; lower weights use different per-kg rates. It estimates basal maintenance needs and does not include deficit or ongoing losses.

name: Alveolar Gas Equation (PAO2)
description: Estimates the alveolar partial pressure of oxygen by the alveolar gas equation, as inspired oxygen fraction times (atmospheric pressure minus water vapor pressure 47) minus arterial CO2 over the respiratory quotient 0.8. It gives ideal alveolar PO2.
notes: FiO2 is a fraction (0.21 for room air), pressures in mmHg, and 47 mmHg is water vapor at body temperature. The 0.8 respiratory quotient is an assumption that varies with diet and metabolism.

name: A-a Oxygen Gradient
description: Computes the alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient by subtracting the measured arterial PaO2 from the alveolar PO2 given by the alveolar gas equation. A widened gradient indicates a problem with gas exchange.
notes: FiO2 is a fraction, all pressures in mmHg. The normal gradient rises with age and with higher FiO2, so interpret the value against age-adjusted expectations.

name: Maximum Dose by Weight
description: Calculates the maximum allowable drug dose by multiplying the maximum dose per kilogram by body weight. It gives the safety ceiling for a weight-based medication.
notes: Maximum dose per kg in mg/kg and weight in kg give a total in mg. Some drugs also have an absolute cap regardless of weight, which this formula does not enforce.

name: Tablets Needed
description: Determines how many tablets to give by dividing the prescribed dose by the strength of one tablet. It converts an ordered dose into a countable number of tablets.
notes: Dose and tablet strength must use the same mass unit so they cancel. A non-integer result may require a different strength or a splittable formulation.

name: Percent to mg/mL Concentration
description: Converts a percent weight-per-volume concentration to mg/mL by multiplying by 10, since 1% w/v equals 1 g per 100 mL, or 10 mg/mL. It is a standard pharmacy conversion.
notes: This assumes a weight/volume percent (grams of solute per 100 mL). It does not apply to weight/weight or volume/volume percentages.

name: Volume from Dose and Concentration
description: Calculates the volume of solution needed to deliver a dose, by dividing the ordered dose by the solution concentration. It converts a mass dose into a measurable liquid volume.
notes: Dose in mg and concentration in mg/mL give a volume in mL. Ensure the concentration reflects the actual vial or diluted preparation being drawn from.

name: Estimated Blood Volume
description: Estimates total blood volume by multiplying body weight by an average blood volume per kilogram. It approximates circulating blood volume for transfusion and blood loss calculations.
notes: Weight in kg and blood volume per kg in mL/kg, roughly 70 for adult men, 65 for women, and higher for neonates. Select the per-kg value appropriate to the patient group.

name: Pack-Years
description: Calculates smoking exposure in pack-years by multiplying the number of packs smoked per day by the number of years smoked. One pack-year equals a pack a day for a year.
notes: Packs per day assumes 20 cigarettes per pack; convert cigarettes per day by dividing by 20. For varying habits, sum pack-years over each period separately.

name: Fractional Excretion of Sodium (FENa)
description: Computes the fractional excretion of sodium as a percent, from urine and serum sodium and creatinine, as (urine sodium times serum creatinine) over (serum sodium times urine creatinine) times 100. It helps distinguish causes of acute kidney injury.
notes: Sodium values and creatinine values must each be in matching units so they cancel. A value below 1% suggests prerenal azotemia; recent diuretic use invalidates the interpretation.

name: Transferrin Saturation
description: Calculates transferrin saturation as a percent, dividing serum iron by total iron-binding capacity and multiplying by 100. It shows what fraction of iron-binding sites are occupied by iron.
notes: Serum iron and TIBC must share the same unit (here ug/dL) so they cancel. Low values suggest iron deficiency and high values iron overload.

name: Absolute Neutrophil Count
description: Calculates the absolute neutrophil count from the white cell count and the combined percentage of segmented and band neutrophils. It quantifies infection-fighting neutrophils and gauges neutropenia risk.
notes: WBC in cells per microliter and the neutrophil and band values as percentages summed then divided by 100. An ANC below 500 indicates severe neutropenia with high infection risk.

name: Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV)
description: Calculates the mean corpuscular volume, the average size of a red blood cell, as hematocrit times 10 divided by the red cell count. The result in femtoliters classifies anemias by cell size.
notes: Hematocrit as a percent and RBC count in millions per microliter; the factor 10 makes the units work out to femtoliters. Low MCV means microcytic and high means macrocytic anemia.

name: Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin (MCH)
description: Calculates the mean corpuscular hemoglobin, the average mass of hemoglobin per red blood cell, as hemoglobin times 10 divided by the red cell count. The result in picograms reflects the hemoglobin content of each cell.
notes: Hemoglobin in g/dL and RBC count in millions per microliter; the factor 10 yields picograms. MCH tends to parallel MCV and is low in iron deficiency.

name: Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin Conc. (MCHC)
description: Calculates the mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration, the hemoglobin concentration within red cells, as hemoglobin divided by hematocrit times 100. It indicates how densely packed hemoglobin is in the cells.
notes: Hemoglobin in g/dL and hematocrit as a percent give a result in g/dL. Low MCHC is hypochromic; abnormally high values can signal spherocytosis or a lab measurement error.

name: Corrected Reticulocyte Count
description: Corrects the reticulocyte percentage for the degree of anemia, multiplying it by the patient's hematocrit divided by a normal hematocrit of 45. It gives a truer picture of bone marrow red cell production.
notes: Reticulocyte and hematocrit both as percents; 45 is the assumed normal hematocrit. The correction prevents overestimating reticulocytosis when the total red cell mass is low.

name: Henderson-Hasselbalch pH
description: Calculates blood pH by the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, as 6.1 plus the base-10 logarithm of bicarbonate divided by dissolved CO2 (0.03 times pCO2). It links the bicarbonate buffer system to blood acidity.
notes: Bicarbonate in mmol/L and pCO2 in mmHg; 6.1 is the pKa of carbonic acid and 0.03 the CO2 solubility factor. It describes the carbonic acid-bicarbonate buffer only.

name: Cardiac Output (Fick)
description: Estimates cardiac output using the Fick principle, dividing whole-body oxygen consumption by the arterial-venous oxygen content difference. That difference is computed from hemoglobin, its oxygen-carrying capacity (1.34 mL O2 per gram), and the arterial minus venous saturations.
notes: Saturations are entered as percentages; the factor 10 converts g/dL to g/L. Result is in L/min. Ignores dissolved oxygen, so it slightly underestimates true content.

name: Karvonen Target Heart Rate
description: Computes a training target heart rate by the Karvonen method: it takes the heart-rate reserve (maximum minus resting rate), scales it by the desired intensity fraction, and adds back the resting rate. The result is the heart rate to aim for during exercise.
notes: Intensity is a fraction between 0 and 1, not a percentage; 0.7 means 70 percent. Accuracy depends on true resting and maximum rates, which are often estimated.

name: One-Rep Max (Brzycki)
description: Estimates the one-repetition maximum (the greatest weight liftable once) from a weight lifted for several repetitions, using the Brzycki formula. It divides the weight by a factor that shrinks as the repetition count rises, so more reps at a given weight imply a higher one-rep max.
notes: Only valid for roughly 1 to 10 reps; accuracy drops sharply at high rep counts and the formula fails at 37 reps (division by zero). It is an estimate, not a measured max.

name: Power-to-Weight Ratio
description: Divides power output by body weight to give the power-to-weight ratio, a key measure of endurance performance in cycling and running. A higher value means more power available per kilogram of body mass.
notes: Both inputs must be instantaneous or averaged over the same interval. Body weight, not total system weight, is used here; add equipment mass separately if needed.

name: METs Energy Expenditure
description: Estimates calories burned during activity from the metabolic equivalent (MET) value, body weight, and duration. It uses the standard relation that one MET equals 3.5 mL of oxygen per kilogram per minute, converting oxygen use into kilocalories.
notes: Assumes a resting metabolic rate of 3.5 mL/kg/min, which varies between people. Duration is in minutes; result is total kcal for the session, not per minute.

name: Running Calorie Expenditure
description: Estimates the energy used while running from body weight and distance, using the approximation that about 1.036 kcal is burned per kilogram of body weight per kilometer run. It depends on distance rather than speed or time.
notes: Gross (not net of resting metabolism) estimate that ignores pace, terrain, and running economy. Distance is in kilometers; the coefficient bakes in typical running efficiency.

name: Cycling Calorie Expenditure
description: Estimates the calories a cyclist burns from average mechanical power, duration, and muscular efficiency. Mechanical work in kilojoules is divided by efficiency to get metabolic energy, which is then converted to kilocalories.
notes: Efficiency is a fraction (about 0.20 to 0.25 for cycling). The factor 3.6 converts watt-hours to kilojoules and 4.184 converts kilojoules to kilocalories.

name: Projectile Sport Range
description: Calculates the horizontal range of a projectile launched over level ground, from launch speed, launch angle, and gravity. Range is the speed squared times the sine of twice the angle, divided by gravitational acceleration.
notes: Angle must be in radians. Ignores air resistance and assumes equal launch and landing heights, so it overestimates real sporting ranges. Maximum range occurs at 45 degrees.

name: Body Mass Index
description: Computes the body mass index by dividing body weight in kilograms by the square of height in meters. BMI is a simple screening figure used to categorize underweight, normal, overweight, and obese ranges.
notes: Height must be in meters, not centimeters. BMI does not distinguish muscle from fat and can mislead for very muscular or elderly people.

name: Allometric Strength Index
description: Scales total weight lifted by body weight raised to the two-thirds power to give an allometric strength index. This adjustment compares strength fairly across athletes of different body sizes, since strength scales roughly with cross-sectional area.
notes: Dimensionless index for ranking only, not an absolute quantity. Uses the two-thirds exponent from geometric scaling; other standards use different exponents.

name: Body Fat (US Navy, Male)
description: Estimates male body-fat percentage from waist, neck, and height using the US Navy circumference method. The logarithm of waist minus neck and the logarithm of height feed an empirical formula tuned to match hydrostatic weighing.
notes: For males only and uses base-10 logarithms; all lengths in centimeters. It is a statistical estimate that can err by several percent for individuals.

name: BMR (Mifflin-St Jeor, Male)
description: Estimates the basal metabolic rate for males using the Mifflin-St Jeor equation, the daily energy the body uses at complete rest. It combines weight, height, and age with fixed coefficients and adds a constant of 5 for males.
notes: Male-specific (the female version subtracts 161 instead of adding 5). Weight in kilograms, height in centimeters, age in years; result is resting energy, before any activity factor.

name: Maximum Heart Rate
description: Estimates the age-predicted maximum heart rate with the classic rule of 220 minus age. It gives an upper bound on heart rate used to set exercise intensity zones.
notes: A rough population average with a standard deviation of about 10 to 12 bpm, so individuals vary widely. Newer formulas like 208 minus 0.7 times age fit data better.

name: Waist-to-Hip Ratio
description: Divides waist circumference by hip circumference to give the waist-to-hip ratio, a standard measure of body fat distribution used to assess health risk.
notes: Measure both circumferences with the same unit and a relaxed, unstretched tape. Higher ratios indicate more abdominal fat and are associated with greater cardiometabolic risk.

name: Mean Arterial Pressure (from Cardiac Output and Peripheral Resistance)
description: Estimates mean arterial pressure (MAP) as the product of cardiac output (CO) and total peripheral resistance (TPR), analogous to Ohm's law (V = I×R) applied to the circulatory system. This relationship underlies how changes in cardiac output or vascular resistance affect blood pressure.
notes: Assumes central venous pressure is negligible (approximately 0 mmHg), which is normally a reasonable approximation; results should be interpreted alongside clinical context, as normal MAP is typically 70-100 mmHg.

name: Total Peripheral Resistance (from MAP and Cardiac Output)
description: Calculates total peripheral resistance (TPR), the resistance the systemic circulation offers to blood flow, by dividing mean arterial pressure (MAP) by cardiac output (CO). This is the inverse relationship of the MAP = CO × TPR equation, analogous to Ohm's law (R = V/I).
notes: Assumes central venous pressure is negligible; elevated TPR is a hallmark of conditions such as essential hypertension, while decreased TPR is seen in states like septic shock.

name: Filtration Fraction (GFR / Renal Plasma Flow)
description: Calculates the filtration fraction, the proportion of renal plasma flow that is filtered across the glomerulus, by dividing the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) by the renal plasma flow (RPF). A normal filtration fraction in healthy kidneys is approximately 0.2 (20%).
notes: Result is expressed as a decimal fraction (multiply by 100 for a percentage); an elevated filtration fraction can occur with efferent arteriolar constriction, while a reduced value can indicate afferent arteriolar constriction or reduced GFR.
